title: Mrs. Charlotte Botney and Mrs. Bertha George McCullum Interview, 1960-10-16
interviewee: Mrs. Charlotte Botney and Mrs. Bertha George McCullum

blocks.x: I told them to bring that carnage yesterday. I've seen these carnage. Well, they didn't tell me nothing about that. I told them to tell them to ram and have it for two weeks. I didn't know anything about it. Because I just asked Mama, she said, there's now some parts, you know. I sure told ram. So I told them that when they get better leave, and she's on her way home, you know, you could follow ram's car, just go down and see it. If you want to see there, it's not sure. If you got real carnage, you know. Yeah, real carnage.
Connate is what they call. Connate. Connate. Connate.
Connate. Conn. Yeah, conn.
Yeah, conn.

It looks so odd, you know, with the long ones they have now. Yeah. Yeah, that's right. I should have. Your jaw is to come over here and sit down and make it. Oh, shit. This is what they do. What's a football game, is it? Yeah.
I don't want to get that on the team. So just how do you spell your name, Ms. McCollum?
M-C-C-U-L-L-U-N. Capital N-C, capital C-U-L-L-U-N.
That's what I wasn't sure. McCollum. Do you remember the date when your husband died, and about when he was born?

Oh, he was born on July 27th, 1884. 1884. Because we were just about 11 months at different times, and I was born the same age we were born. And he's from there, it's going to be 40 years now. About almost 40 years. Yeah, the 14th of next month. 14th of next month. Yeah, 1920.

1920. Oh, I didn't know it was that far back. Yeah, 1920. Because of your son that played too. My son played music too. So, if people get mixed up in all of them, they don't even know them. Even to George McCollum. And some of the younger people don't know about your husband.
George D. George D. George D. George D. George D.
George D. Junior. You know my son.
Yeah, yeah. We were on the road.
Yeah. That's where people get mixed up, where you never know if they're talking about your husband or your son. My son and dad.

Well, they're both parents. My son's dead too. But the daddy died in 1920. November 14th. When was your son born? Oh, Derek. He was born on the 22nd of February, in 1906. 1906. The 22nd of February, 1906. And then when did he die about? He died in March. 1938. 1938. 1938.
That's not the offering loan. March the 19th. 21st. The 21st. 1938. 22 years ago. Yeah, 22 years ago.
But then? 22 years ago. Yeah.
But daddy is one of the original founders of James. Oh, yes, I knew that.

People told us about Professor Annette. Professor Annette. Oh, Amanda? Have you seen Amanda? Oh, you have a lot of. I'm sure he came by my place this afternoon. I'd like to see. He stops by when he goes to church for an open. We like to see. Oh, he and George, they play music.

I thought we had to play so much together. And he'd follow George home and I'd get mad and put them all out. Those were some days. That's the band that was not in the building. Oh, yeah. Now that's my grandson, George McCollum.
He didn't keep up your mute. He's a job. He's a piece of the paper.
It has the old banner from McCollum's Jazz Orchestra. First organized in the, it says here, the first New Orleans marching band organized

in the 1890s. George McCollum's first. First organized in the first New Orleans marching band organized in the 1890s by George McCullen I. The banner presented by George McCullen IV already. They got the fifth one too.
They have the fifth one. I'm losing now.
That's the same old banner they had all those years. Way back, is it that French band? Oh yeah, I've seen that.
Yeah, they gave me that in the Hall of France. That's the copy of Jasmine. Yes. The Bucket Book copy.

They have some of those with pictures in too. That's the one that came out in the army. They have some of those with pictures but they never had a picture of your husband in it though. I don't think they didn't have anything.
Well I was getting a picture for you with his little short. With his short. Would you like to have one of them?
We can make copies of those too by the way so that you don't have to give up your original.
No, we have a lot of them.
Well we'd appreciate that if we could have one.
We have a lot of them.

You have one. Yes, I have one of those. So I'm guessing on that. Can you tell us some more about your husband where he was raised? Did he was born and raised right here in the city? Right here in the office.
He was born and raised right here.
Did he ever tell you who his teachers were? Or did he have teachers when he was younger?

Well, I'll tell you. My uncle was the, he's still living an old man in the convalescent home in California. Thomas R. LeBlanc. He taught him. Oh, I've heard of him. My uncle. That's my own uncle. I think I have a picture of him in the. Here's him.
And I've got, what's the right up from him? He is over 90 years old. Yes.
That's his picture. I think it's a picture that he played maybe in the, Henry Allen's band.

Henry Allen's, well, Allen used to play, George used to play with Allen. My husband and Allen, all of them, they all played together. John Robichaux and all those musicians, old musicians. My uncle and John Robichaux were the two leading old musicians. You know, Robichaux and, well, I think Dave Perkins too. Yes, he was. Dave Perkins. Oh, yes.
And that's with his, his little sharp trumpet.

Oh, yeah. That's his picture. That was a con. Yeah, that's all they used in the middle. That's all they used in those days. Yes, that's the most popular one. Almost all of them did. Yes, he used to come.
And you knew that Joe Oliver did. Yeah.

Well, I just laughed and talked about Joe. We were just talking about Joe. And some of them boys, you know, he taught. Did you say he taught Joe Oliver? He taught Joe. He taught Joe. And many times, he'd give somebody else a present. I'd say, well, they never say nothing about Joe, Steve and Joe. And I know that. He taught Joe and Joe played in his brass band. And when he got the string band, as they call in those days, and used to play out of the lake for all the country clubs and all the places out of the lake. Joe used to go with him and with the boys. And that's how he learned how to play the string instrument, you see. And they would all throw in and give Joe money so he could go with them. Yeah. Well, I know that myself. My children was all small. I know that.
We talked to Mrs. Oliver, Joe Oliver's wife, Mrs. Stella Oliver. Yeah. She couldn't remember the name of his teacher.

She couldn't remember. Well, George taught him. I know that much. George taught him. I don't know who else taught him. I know. I'd ask him if Mrs. Perkins and he said no. I know that. And he taught him. He taught him how to play in the string music. With the string music. And I said often he'd come. But they're always in my home. I knew them well. I knew all of them. I knew all of them. Manuel Moneta is another one.
Yes. He talks about your husband.
He talks about George all the time.
He used to call him horse. Yeah, he called a horse.

Yeah. He used to call him horse. He used to call him horse. He used to call him horse. And I was talking about Manuel. I said I'd like to see Manuel. I hadn't seen him in a long time. And when they'd go play, they'd play out of the lake and come back, they'd grab him in the rainboard and George would be just coming home and sitting on Louisiana Avenue car and go to sleep. And they would bring him to the river, bring him back to Canal Street. And then when he'd come back and start the car stop, Franklin and Louisiana, they'd come up and wake him up and tell him, Go get off your corner, Mac. There's your corner. And wake him up. I said, Joe. He said, me and the horse had been walking from Farron Teller's, from Farron Teller up to the fair. And we'd get to the fair and we'd come back and walk again. I said, that's all you and Manuel can do. And when he'd get ready to come back, George, they would stand on the, wouldn't come in. They were scared because I'd call him out. I'd call him out. There wasn't but one of them. And I didn't know if you knew Manuel, Honorary Dutre. He was a slide with Eddie Atkins that played, now Eddie Atkins is another performer who played with my husband, slide drum. And Dutre. Honorary Dutre. I know Sam Dutre.
You know Sam. Yeah.
And his dad too. And Pete, you know Pete Dutre. Yeah. Well all of Dutres played with George.
Now for years, Daddy played for the Jefferson City Buzzards. Oh. Many, many years in the carnival tree.

And he played until he died. They still don't know if he did. The Jefferson City Buzzards. And he played for them every time. That's a long day, though. Yeah. And he played for the Jefferson City Buzzards.
Almost up to the time of his death, would you say?
Almost up to the time of his death.
Almost up to 1920 then.

That's right. Well when he took sick, he played that Bulls Parade. And I didn't want him to go play, he was sick. He was 26. He got out of the band when he played the Bulls Parade and come home and got the band. Then the Monday, he had an Artfellas Parade across the river. And I begged him. And this child's godfather played too in the band. And he begged, he said, George, don't go play that Bulls Parade. I'll give you that $10 out of my pocket. He said, no Brown, my word is my bond. And he went and played. I wouldn't get calling to get his breakfast the Monday morning to play that Artfellas Parade across the river. And he said, birthday, why didn't you call me? I said, because I don't want you to go play that parade. And he says to me, I fixed his breakfast, sit down in his breakfast. He says, do you know, you don't want me to go play that parade? He said, but that would be the last parade I'll play. He said, let me go and play that parade. I didn't bother. He come home and got in the bathing up and he said, well, he died. That was in July. And he died in November. And that was the last parade he played. When did he die? 1920. 1920. 1920. November the 14th. 40 years. 40 years. The 14th of next month. Long time ago. Yeah. That's long.
Did he have any other teachers or did he?

Well, as I tell you, my uncle brought them out. It's youngsters. All of them was about 14 and 15. I don't believe that one of them was 16 years old. They had just a band of little boys. So they brought them out. Him and Kenchon. Dave Perkins used to help them. I've heard that name Kenchon. Who is that? Oh. What was his first name? He was a musician. He and my uncle were friends.
Monk Johnson mentioned him once but I never did get that. I can't think of him in that song.

But they were the one that started these little boys out in this brass band for parades. Was he here in the city? Kenchon? Yeah, Kenchon was right here in the city. He and my uncle were friends. Now I can't think of his first name.
Did he play a some, a carnet or something?
He played an instrument too. Uncle played alto. My uncle played alto. But he was a real musician. He taught music.
You don't know what Kenchon played?

No, I don't know what, I can't remember. But I do remember the first parade they played was on the, in May. It was, was it the Odd Colors parade? They used to parade. And that day, that morning they had the eclipse of the sun and everything went dark. I remember that. Because we was living then on 7th street between Ramport and Drives. 1912. And Uncle brought that little, and Kenchon brought that band out to all those boys. There was my husband. There was Cheap, Laura's husband. What's his last name? Cheap, one eye. Can't call his name, no. And, it was him. He had one eye. And, no, his eyes was kind of blue. Was he a bass man? No, he, that's played, not in your time. I don't even know, in either of George's time. That was in my husband's time. I'm trying to call them young boys in the band. Somebody by the name of Clem that played Cornette, I think, had one eye.
Clem? Clem. Clem.

Clem. That's, that name's familiar too. I remember that name. Clem. Oh, yes. Clem, he had a son with his son with me. Yeah. Eddward Clem. All of them was in my uncle's class and my husband come along, a young boy under them. They had the Indiana Brass Band then. The Indiana. The Indiana Brass Band. See? And George, and who else? George was the youngest carnet player in the band. My George. He was the youngest in the band. Now, he was always with those older men. With my uncle, Ken Schoen, Dave Poitkin, John Robichaud, all of those men.
By the way, when did you get married to Mr. I got married in 1905.
April the 27th. 1905.
So he was about 21 years old then. He was 21.

We just made our 21 the next July. Both of us. Where did you live then? Was that up on 7th Street around there? No, I lived, when we got married, I lived with his mother on Liberty Street, between 6th and Washington. And he'd been raised up in that neighborhood then? Right then, right around, and then lived no further down than 2nd Street. I think he was born on 2nd Street. 2nd between Liberty and Howard, I believe. Somewhere along in there.
Did he ever mention another trumpet player, Buddy Bolden, or did you ever hear him?
Oh no, he didn't play with Buddy. Buddy was out of the class. Buddy played, but he didn't play with Buddy.
Do you remember hearing Buddy Bolden yourself?
Oh, I know Buddy Bolden. I know his sister, his mother, and all of them. Oh really? I know. I know.
I talked to Buddy Bolden's widow one time. Yeah. And she told me a little bit about his mother and all too. About his mother. I knew his mother and his sister. But not very much.
But, um, I don't think he played music too very long when he took sick of all the time. Yeah, she lost his mind. Yeah, he lost his mind.

That would be two years after you were married. Yeah, mm-hmm. That's what I'm telling you. I don't know too much about him. He didn't rather play music with George, because George didn't play that time.
Do you remember going down to the dances that Buddy Bolton played?

No, they didn't allow me to go to dances. That's things. They didn't allow me to go to dances. I was in school. I went to the big picnics. Yes. And George would come and ask my uncle. The same uncle taught him music if I was living with them. And I'm down even school in the country. And he'd tell them, no, all the clubs, and I'd think, I'll bring her there. You'll see her at the dance. Will they bring the dance? Girls didn't run the streets like they do now.

That's the one that would be nice to interview. Before he'd be, you know, he is still in his 90s. Yeah, my uncle. But he knew the origin of a lot of... Oh, I have a lot of things that went on here. Yeah, Dixie Land Jazz.
Two years ago in August, Professor Mineta and I went out to California.
He was able then to really know.
Yeah, we didn't know it. We didn't know it. We didn't know it.
We were there two years ago.
We went to two years ago. We stayed with Johnny St. Cyr. Remember, he used to live not far from here.
Yeah. The guitarist there is here. He had a symphony orchestra out in Hollywood.
He taught music when he was out there. He had an old boys and kids orchestra. Played in Hollywood. That's what he did in California, taught music.
We saw quite a few of the California musicians. Like Kidore is out there. Oh, yeah. He's out there. Ed Garland, some of the other members of the band. But I never knew your uncle.
I saw Bob Johnson before he died. Uncle took me to see him in Los Angeles. Got to see him after that. Yes, 1949.
Anyway, I'm sorry that your uncle isn't able to...
Oh, no, not now. He's in the convalescent home. He don't remember anything. No.
He talks about the past, but he rattles off. He rattles off.
He was older than your husband.
Oh, he was in his 90s. He was in his 90s.
In his 90s, sure.
But Daddy did a lot of writing, too. He did a lot of arrangements, you call that. Arranges.
Well, he never... He arranged... He'd go buy a sheet of music from the music store, and he'd take that sheet of music and arrange that for his whole brass band. His whole band. His whole band.
He wrote his own music. He had two bands. He had a string band and a brass band.
He arranged his own music. Do you know how that term string band got started? Of course, I know they're using guitars.
I don't know why it started.
But they still had a carnet and clarinet.
They still had a carnet, clarinet, and bass violin, and trombones. Trombones. Trombones in it. Bass violin. Sometimes they'd use a guitar.
Yeah. Of course, that's a string instrument.
That's a string instrument.
That's a string instrument. Yeah. Yeah. You know why? Because, you see, the street band didn't use no string instrument. No, at all.
It was a brass band.
Yeah, it was a brass band. Often, they used a string instrument, so they called them a string band.
It must be that. It was a mixture. Yeah. But I didn't know why, you know.
But for a long time, they used to have string trios, too, you know, like violin and guitar and bass. Yeah.

Well, often Joe Robinson, don't you remember? Yes. Piano, some white people would hire them. They'd want just a piano and a violin and a bass or violin, something like that. Soft music would tell Joe, well, I don't want, I want your piano player. Well, Naomi Franklin played piano with Joe. Did you know her? Naomi, she was a Miss Barrett.
I don't think I know.

You didn't know the Franklin? She was a very famous woman until she went down. Oh, yeah. Now, you didn't know her. Well, she played piano with him. Now she was a George. And what's this other girl who used to play piano with him at times? That's before Harold's time. Before Harold's time. See, Harold came along with Bill George. Bill George. Yeah, Bill George and Allison. Bill George and Allison. Yeah. And that was in George's time. Yeah.

It was, well, everything was fine then because whenever they would, you know, play jobs and whatnot, they'd always stop in front of the house, you know. I can remember thinking we'd all run out as children, you know. And they'd have this, they would play in wagons and trucks and things and whatnot, you know. Old furniture wagons. Old furniture wagons and whatnot, you know. And then they would have them pass our house. And frankly, between Louise and Eve and Darrell Shays, and they'd stop and play us a number, you know. I've heard how they advertise. It's real fun. Yeah. If it's real fun.
Just for your... And all that rehearsal in my house, which every fall, I'd give you...
That's all we can remember. One room that rehearsed. All we can remember from Papa's to Little George, you know. You did us. Having a band in the house playing. And we could sleep through all that.
Sleep through all. Did he ever compose any numbers of his own?

Who, my husband? Yeah. No. Not that I know of him. If he did, I don't remember. But, Lord, he had all kinds of music. After he died, I had a big box of music. I told him, Mama, that would have been so useful now. Oh, I know. The Lord, the Reigners. Now you don't know it. Money. My son had some of the music. Some of the copies before he died. And he used to say to me, he made me start all of his music out. And he said, put out the valuable music. He says, now, don't you let nobody take this. Someday you might need a piece of bread. Tell me. You might need a piece of bread and you can sell that. Yeah. But I turned all that over to George, my son. Don't know what that's.
Well, maybe somebody got some good out of it, I hope.
I hope because I hope he got too good of it.

Yeah, because my brother would have been a famous musician anyway. Yes, he must have. He was a wonderful trumpet musician. He was famous when he was in the middle. He was famous. If he could hold a note, you're talking about Louis Armstrong holding a note. But little George could hold that note. And I'm sure he would have been real famous. He was only 32 when he died.

Only 32. Yes. He used to play with Henry Jr. or I said, but it's Clare that same, the fine Clare that same woman on the music box. But George was playing that legit dance on Crandelet and Canal. Right on that call. Yeah, he played seven years. He cut a record. He was working every day when he was playing a really bad night.

Well, George cut an old-time record. Millen Boy George. Yeah, yeah, he did. Oh, did he make some records? Yes, he made Millen Boy George. That's your record. Uh-huh, uh-huh. My sister was telling me about that yesterday.
Do you remember what brand, what label, as they call it?
No, I don't. I don't. My older sister was telling me that yesterday.
Yeah, he made a record.
That he made this Millen Boy George. He in town. He in town. Uh-huh.
You don't know if anybody might have the record?
I don't know.

Sometimes they'd record those and they wouldn't bring them out. Yeah, that's right. Just die right there. They never would have to issue it. But it was Millen Boy George. We could find that. Oh, that would be wonderful.
Maybe somebody... We could try. We could try. She told me about it yesterday with those old-time recording places, maybe. Then maybe you think Lola would know.

Oh, Lola never knows. I've collected records for years. I've been trying to say Lola's lost of mine. I don't know if it's that. He had his own band at the time. He had his own band at the time. He had his own band at the time. Then she wouldn't let Junior keep on with his music.

And it was the year when they first started having... We used to trail them everywhere, you know. The first started having sectional. The saxophones would stand at one time. They used to use their hats for mufflers, you know. And I remember they just started and everybody had to turn to sing. And Lola couldn't sing. I never will forget that. That was just coming out. And to get to hear them say a little line, you know, to sing a little line.
He didn't sing and he didn't know how to dance. He didn't know how to dance. He was just coming out. All you know is that music. He didn't know how to dance.

Picture George being a big man. I don't know if George was a little punitive thing. Oh, yeah. Let me show you. Yeah. I got one of the pictures which that's the one he's going to try to throw off. Yeah. Oh, he's trying to throw it off. Small, small. Well, good. The George is on it. Good.
Are we going to see some of this?
I'll get a copy for you. I'll get it. I hope it'll be big enough to see. Yeah. I wonder, did your husband make any records? No. They didn't make many before 1921. They didn't buy them.

At that time. They didn't buy them. All he worked like Mike Houston. Yeah. He transferred music into this and this. This one we have on the... He taught a good minute. He taught quite a bit too. Alvin Alpool. He taught Alvin. He taught Alvin. Everything you know. He taught Alvin. He taught Alvin. He taught Alvin. Yeah, the album too.
That's right. A little bit of that. A little bit of that. A little bit of that. Yeah, yeah.

You know what, Finnis George, when he fell through the hatch hole in a half million years, he never took care of himself. And he couldn't. He never done it. One trumpet, one trumpet. And he played that trumpet.
And he played that trumpet. Yeah, yeah. I'm telling you, it's just a ball.
Did your husband have any other job in the daytime working any other? Oh, yes, he worked in a cotton, a graduate, what you call it, every day, he played music every night.
That's right, he told us. Yeah, cotton sample, too.
That's right, I remember Mineta.
Yeah, did Mineta, a manual day.
And now he got somebody else a job once, too. Let me see, who did he get a job? Some other musician.
Oh, he was crazy about Daddy, though.

Man, Mineta was crazy about Daddy. I mean, how your father got somebody else a job working with him, though. Oh, he had a job. What was that? Remember, he said... I don't remember, now he got another musician in there for a while.

I know he was there for a while, he didn't stay that long. Because, you know, that fella from away from New York, he stayed that long then. I do remember the story, but I can't think of a name. You can't think of a name.
I remember one time, Professor Mineta told us they played at one of the big restaurants, like Antoine's or... Oh, they...
All down in the Duke Array.

One night they had a bass player there, Dan Lee Lewis, and they made some jokes about him, and this fella didn't like it. No. So when it was all over, Fass didn't know what it was all about. He didn't know you had to bend the fella, so the bass player was gonna hit the manual maneta. Yeah. And your husband stepped in between and... Oh, he had a temper. He fired him. He fired him. He fired him from the band.
Oh, yeah. He had a temper. He used to take that little shot, uh, or, con out of his and fight him.

Yeah. He didn't like it. He had a charm with him. He didn't care if he did. He didn't care if he did. It was anybody. Yeah. Don't worry. He wouldn't think of us. He was very, very stern. Yeah. He stopped his fight. But don't worry, cause he was ready to knock you if you said anything.

I remember he came home one day and he said about, um, a blind man, you know, had asked him for money. He was sitting down and he was leaving his work. And, uh, he wasn't far from that blind man when the blind man got up to go and borrow him, you know, to spend his money. And he wasn't killing him. Yeah. No.
That was, uh,
He never, uh, he never advocated, you know, giving it to blind people on the street and whatnot. He said, He said,
I was gonna ask you, had you mentioned that your husband was with, um, a circus band? Yes.
Which one was? Ringling Brothers.
Ringling Brothers.

Mm-hmm. Now I came to the two people that, uh, uh, came to engage him to go with this circus. There was the man and his wife that worked for him. They were musicians. And he was the captain building then and they left and, uh, and went with him. He stayed two months traveling. And he said, I used to tell me I get tired of going to bed in one time and getting up in another. I'm coming home. And the only way that they would let him come back home. And he, he, he called, he called me up and said, say, you send me a telegram to come home at once. I went down to the Western Union to send him the telegram that night to come home. And the, and the man, the man that took the message, he said, what George Jr. in Kansas? In that city, Kansas. And they just holler. And you tell George, you come on home. All the white people knew him and not being in a room. Yeah. Well George Jr. in that city, Kansas. I say, you part of the circus from here and I don't want to come home. I, the only way they wouldn't even pay if they didn't want to leave, even get in position.
And he said, well I'm coming home.

And she was just a year old. And when he comes back home, she didn't recognize him right away. And that just, he said, I'm never in the ball. I was his aunt. He was, he was dying almost. And, and, and he got up by the way. And he was, and he was dying almost.

And, and, and he got up out of bed and we stole out. And Mama went to the market. And, and we stole out and we made all around. He took me, you know, he used to like race horses. And he took me by Pratt's and by the people who had his diamonds. Farron Tellers.
Farron Tellers.
And made a round of all the places where he used to go downtown, you know. And then he came back home. Was the last time.

Well, Emmanuel didn't tell you how he, he used to go to the fire and tell them in the jobs. He had beautiful eyes. He got all over the jobs. And he followed Emmanuel to the ferryman. You never told him about that, did he? He didn't tell you all about that? No. I can tell everybody. He wasn't very old when he died at all. He was 46, is that right? No. No. No. No, he was 30. 36. 36. 36. That's the age of 36. 36. That's a million. Billion. Billion. Billion.

36, you know. Because you lived there quite a while ago. I always think of him like an old man. Yeah. Yeah. An old man. Because he's the old man. Yes. Because they would be the same age. Yes. Mama 76. Yeah, I'm 76 since July. He was a real young man when he died. Yeah. And that famous already when he's only 36. Yeah. Yeah. How long did he stay with the circus, did you say?

Just two months to stay with him. Just the chart time. Short time, he got tired of that. He said he wasn't used to going to Bain one town, getting up to another. Uh-uh. He said, once we finish, the circus would be moving. He said, he's traveling all the time. He said, uh-uh. I'm coming home. Did he ever go to Chicago or any place to play up there? Oh, yes. Not to Chicago.

He went up there on physical. Quite a few of the bands were like Joe Oliver, you know, went up there while the guys stayed. Joe went up there all the time and stayed. Joe just had his wife and when Joe left, you know, I don't know if he and his wife was together.
They stayed together quite a while. They stayed together. I think they finally did separate in late years. When he died, Joe was over in Savannah. She was back here.

I didn't know too much about her, but I knew him long before he ever got married because he was in my house all the time with my husband. All those young boys. And most of them weren't married. No. As I say, they'd just flock and that's all he was, his work and his music too.
Most of the time he had his own band. Most of the time.
The string band and his brass band.
Both. Both. Do you remember they played any certain clubs or something a long time? I don't know, in those days they played all over town.

segments.title: Opening chatter and spelling the McCullum name
segments.summary: Family small talk before the interview begins; the interviewer asks how to spell McCullum.

segments.title: Dates of birth and death of George McCullum Sr. and his son
segments.summary: Mrs. McCullum gives her husband's birth (1884) and death (Nov. 14, 1920) and her son George Jr.'s birth (1906) and death (1938), clearing up husband versus son.

segments.title: Founder of the brass band; the old McCullum banner and photographs
segments.summary: Charlotte says her father was an original founder of jazz bands; they look at the old McCullum's band banner and discuss copies of pictures.

segments.chapter: Learning music and the early bands
segments.title: George Sr.'s upbringing and his teacher, Uncle Thomas LeBlanc
segments.summary: Born and raised in New Orleans, he was taught by Mrs. McCullum's uncle Thomas LeBlanc, who played with Robichaux, Perkins and Henry Allen's band.

segments.chapter: Learning music and the early bands
segments.title: George Sr. taught Joe Oliver and the string band
segments.summary: She insists her husband taught Joe Oliver, who played in his brass band and learned string music with his string band; Manuel Manetta also talks about him.

segments.chapter: Learning music and the early bands
segments.title: Manuel Manetta, the Dutres and Eddie Atkins
segments.summary: Stories of Manetta ('the horse') falling asleep on the streetcar after playing out at the lake, and of the Dutres and Eddie Atkins who played with George.

segments.chapter: Learning music and the early bands
segments.title: Playing for the Jefferson City Buzzards until his last parade in 1920
segments.summary: He played carnival parades for the Jefferson City Buzzards until he took sick; she describes the last parade he played in July before dying in November 1920.

segments.chapter: Learning music and the early bands
segments.title: LeBlanc and Kenchon start the boys' brass band; Indiana Brass Band
segments.summary: Her uncle and Kenchon brought out a band of boys about 1912, including George as youngest cornetist; she tries to name the members.

segments.chapter: Learning music and the early bands
segments.title: Marriage in 1905 and where they lived
segments.summary: They married April 27, 1905, at about 21, and lived with his mother on Liberty Street.

segments.chapter: Learning music and the early bands
segments.title: Buddy Bolden: not played with, but his family known
segments.summary: George did not play with Bolden, but she knew his mother and sister and says he lost his mind; she was not allowed to go to dances as a girl.

segments.chapter: Learning music and the early bands
segments.title: Uncle LeBlanc and Johnny St. Cyr in California
segments.summary: The interviewer visited California musicians; the uncle, now over 90 in a convalescent home, can no longer remember, and Charlotte saw Bob Johnson in Los Angeles in 1949.

segments.title: Arranging music and the string band versus the brass band
segments.summary: George arranged sheet music for his bands; they discuss why a band is called a string band, its instrumentation, and piano players who worked with small groups.

segments.title: Band rehearsals at home and George's music
segments.summary: Charlotte recalls bands passing the house on wagons and rehearsals in the house; Mrs. McCullum says he composed nothing she knew of but left a box of music.

segments.title: Little George's career, records and teaching Alvin
segments.summary: Charlotte praises her brother little George's trumpet and talks of his seven years at a Canal Street job and an old-time record; he taught Alvin.

segments.title: George Sr.'s day job, his temper and a fired bass player
segments.summary: He worked days in cotton while playing nights; the interviewer relays Manetta's story of a fight with a bass player, whom George fired, and they recall his stern temper.

segments.title: Joining the Ringling Brothers circus band
segments.summary: George went with a circus for two months, got homesick and had his wife wire for him to come home; Charlotte recalls his last tour of his haunts.

segments.title: Joe Oliver goes to Chicago; George's own bands
segments.summary: Joe Oliver went up to Chicago and stayed; she knew him from her house before he married, and George had his own string and brass bands.

segments.title: Where George played: country clubs, halfway house, carnival parades
segments.summary: He played country clubs, the Halfway House, dances at West End and carnival parades for the Jefferson City Buzzards; cornet was his only instrument.

segments.title: George's father and Professor LeBlanc's later life
segments.summary: George's father, also George McCullum, played cornet; they spell LeBlanc, who played alto, lived in Chicago and California and taught children.

segments.title: George insisted on reading notes; Alvin as his student
segments.summary: He made his players learn the music rather than play by ear, which is why his pupils were good musicians, including Alvin.

segments.title: Credit for bringing out Joe Oliver
segments.summary: She complains George gets no credit for teaching Oliver, who became famous by leaving for Chicago; the band members chipped in to pay Joe.

segments.title: Louis Warnick, alto saxophonist with Piron and Tio
segments.summary: They discuss Louis Warnick, who played alto sax with Piron and Lorenzo Tio and died in the 1950s, and Eddie Atkins.

segments.title: Little George in the street band, a powerhouse
segments.summary: Charlotte and her mother recall the street band little George played with and that, like his father, he held up the whole brass band.

segments.title: Little George starts on trumpet; Joe Howard
segments.summary: Little George began music at about 14, studied briefly with Joe Howard, and went on his own; Joe Howard was a fine trumpeter.

segments.title: The Indiana Brass Band and parades for funerals
segments.summary: Puzzling over the name of the Indiana Brass Band, which George joined as the youngest around 1905; bands played big parades and funerals.

segments.title: George's deathbed promise and Catholicism; Mrs. McCullum's health
segments.summary: Before he died George asked that the children be raised Catholic and she converted; she is 76 with high blood pressure.

segments.title: Photographs and the copper printing cut of George Sr.
segments.summary: They talk about when the portrait with his cornet was taken and who holds the copper cut made for a newspaper; his mother said he would rather play than eat.

segments.title: Little George's playing style, lip and the WPA band
segments.summary: Charlotte describes her brother's held notes, range, Dixieland and reading ability, and the last time his mother heard him with the WPA band.

segments.title: The copper cut and how it is used
segments.summary: The interviewer examines the copper printing cut, how it is used for newspapers and how to preserve it; Charlotte notes books omit little George.

segments.title: The circus photograph and uniform
segments.summary: They date the circus-band photograph to 1911, when Charlotte was a year old, and describe his plumed hat and braided uniform.

segments.title: Charlotte's family and the three Georges
segments.summary: Charlotte's son lives in California; they sort out George I, II and III, a grandson in the reserve band holding his grandfather's last cornet.

segments.title: Cornet versus trumpet and Armstrong wanting little George's gold trumpet
segments.summary: A cornet is harder to blow than a trumpet; Armstrong wanted to buy little George's gold trumpet, which was stolen; she kept her husband's cornet.

segments.title: Directions to the house and arrangements
segments.summary: Side conversation giving driving directions to Charlotte's house.

segments.title: Old band uniforms and Papa's banner
segments.summary: They describe the old blue braided uniforms with mandarin collars and ask about the whereabouts of the banner.

segments.title: The banner at the Newport jazz festival and the museum
segments.summary: The banner went to the jazz festival at Newport and little George's son was interviewed; it is kept in the museum.

segments.title: Places little George played: cabarets, Franklin Street and Jackson Avenue
segments.summary: Charlotte recalls where little George played in the 1920s, including a Jackson Avenue place with Steve Lewis where his gold watch was stolen.

segments.title: Bolden's family again
segments.summary: Asked more about Bolden's family, she knew his mother and sister, who lived near her mother-in-law on Second Street.

segments.title: Raymond Brown, little George's friend
segments.summary: Charlotte asks about Raymond Brown, a drummer and her brother's close friend; her mother knows little about him.

segments.title: Little George's wake and funeral crowds
segments.summary: Charlotte describes the huge wake for little George, musicians white and black filling the house after the Steamer President job, since he had played many funerals.
